title: Indica, Sativa, Hybrid: What the Labels Really Tell You
description: The three-bucket system is a rough guide, not a rule. Here is how to read it.

data.text: Most menus sort flower into indica, sativa, and hybrid. It is a useful shorthand for browsing, but the effect you feel has more to do with a product’s cannabinoid and terpene mix than the bucket it lands in.

items: Indica-labeled products are often chosen for evenings and rest.
Sativa-labeled products are often chosen for daytime and activity.
Hybrids sit somewhere in between, leaning one way or the other.

data.text: Two plants with the same label can feel different. If a specific product worked for you, note the brand, the strain name, and the terpene list — that combination is a better predictor than the category alone.

title: How to Read a Certificate of Analysis
description: Every batch is lab-tested. Here is what the numbers on the COA mean.

data.text: A Certificate of Analysis, or COA, is the lab report for a specific batch. Licensed products carry one, and it is worth a glance before you buy.

items: Total THC and total CBD — the potency you are actually paying for.
Pass/fail on pesticides, heavy metals, and residual solvents.
Batch date — fresher flower generally tastes better.

data.text: If a percentage on the shelf tag looks far off from the COA, ask staff. The batch report is the source of truth.

title: Terpenes 101: The Part of the Plant You Can Smell
description: Terpenes shape aroma and may nudge the overall experience.

data.text: Terpenes are aromatic compounds found across the plant world — in citrus peel, pine sap, lavender, and black pepper, among many others. Cannabis makes a lot of them, and they are why two jars can smell nothing alike.
Common ones you will see on labels

items: Myrcene — earthy, musky; often in products marketed for rest.
Limonene — bright, citrus; often in daytime products.
Caryophyllene — peppery; the one that also acts on the body’s CB2 receptors.

data.text: If you keep gravitating toward the same smell, look for that terpene at the top of the list on your next visit.

title: Edibles: Start Low, Go Slow
description: Onset is slow and the dose is easy to misjudge. A simple approach.

data.text: Eaten cannabis is processed by the liver before it reaches you, which is why it can take one to two hours to feel and why it often feels stronger than the same dose inhaled.

items: Take 2.5 to 5mg and set a timer for two hours.
Do not add more until the timer is up.
Have plain snacks and water on hand.

data.text: If you take too much, it is uncomfortable but not dangerous. Find a calm spot, hydrate, and wait it out.

title: Storing Cannabis So It Lasts
description: Light, air, and heat are what degrade flower. Slow them down.

data.text: Cannabinoids and terpenes break down over time. You cannot stop it, but good storage buys you months.

items: Keep flower in an airtight glass jar, not a plastic bag.
Store it somewhere cool, dark, and dry — a drawer, not a windowsill.
Skip the freezer; it makes trichomes brittle.

data.text: Gummies and tinctures are more forgiving, but still keep them out of direct sun and away from heat.

title: Your First Dispensary Visit: What to Expect
description: Bring ID, know roughly what you want, and ask questions.

data.text: Order online ahead of time and pickup is usually a few minutes. Walking in works too — staff can point you in the right direction.

items: A valid, unexpired government photo ID.
A medical card, if you are shopping the medical menu.
A rough budget and format in mind.

data.text: Prices on the menu include what you will pay at the counter unless your state adds tax at checkout. Staff can tell you which applies.
